passages.text: Voting in public was once defended as the honest way of doing it. A man who would not say aloud which candidate he supported was thought to have something to hide, and the open poll, in which each voter declared his choice to a clerk in front of the room, was presented as a safeguard against fraud. It had the opposite effect, and everybody involved knew as much. An employer could stand at the back and watch; a landlord could read the published poll book afterwards and see how his tenants had voted; a creditor could make the connection between a vote and a debt without ever having to say so. The argument for secrecy therefore had to be made against a genuine principle rather than against plain corruption, and it took the better part of the nineteenth century. What carried it in the end was not an appeal to privacy but an observation about power. A vote that can be seen is a vote that can be bought, because the buyer needs proof of delivery; make the proof impossible and the market collapses of its own accord. The modern ballot is built around that insight and not around the voter's feelings. The booth, the uniform paper, the ban on photographing a marked paper and the rule that a spoiled ballot is replaced rather than corrected all exist to make it impossible for a voter to prove how he voted, even when he wants to. Secrecy here is not a right the voter may waive. It is a duty the state imposes on him for everybody else's protection.

A trademark looks like a piece of property and began as a piece of consumer protection. Before the nineteenth century most goods were bought from a person who had made them or who could at least be found if they failed, and the buyer's protection was the seller's presence. Industrial production removed that protection. A tin of something arrived in a town from a factory three hundred miles away, and the question of whom to blame if the contents were bad had no obvious answer. The mark on the tin was the answer. It did not say that the contents were good; it said who was answerable for them, which allowed a reputation to be built and, far more importantly, to be lost. Courts that enforced marks in this period said as much explicitly: the wrong being punished was deceiving the public, not taking something from the manufacturer. Modern law has been pulled a long way from that position by a simple commercial fact, which is that a mark with a reputation is worth money in itself. Once that is true the mark is defended as an asset, and arguments appear that have nothing to do with any buyer being misled: dilution, tarnishment, protection against uses in unrelated trades where no customer could possibly be confused. None of this is absurd and some of it is necessary. But it is worth noticing how far the justification has travelled, because the public interest that produced the law in the first place is now one consideration among several, and it is not always the one that wins.

Every other experimental discipline can repeat its experiments. Archaeology cannot, because the act of excavating a site is the act of taking it apart. The information is not in the objects but in their arrangement: which layer a thing lay in, what was above it and below it, how the soil around it had been disturbed. Once the trench is open and the earth has been removed, that arrangement exists only in the record the excavator chose to make, and no later scholar can go back and check a question the excavator did not think to ask. This is why the discipline is so preoccupied with documentation that outsiders find it eccentric, and why it is the only field in which deliberately not working on a site is a respectable research decision. Several of the best-known sites have been left partly undug, on the explicit ground that future methods will extract more from the same soil than present ones can. That judgement has been vindicated more than once already: material shovelled away as spoil in the 1930s would now yield seeds, pollen, residues and dates. The uncomfortable corollary is that a great deal of what was excavated in the first century of the discipline is, for most purposes, lost. The objects sit in museum cases and the sites are gone, and what we have of their context is whatever one person wrote in one notebook, by the standards of a time that could not know what would later be worth recording.

The common-sense account of famine is that there is not enough food. It is very often wrong, and the mistake has cost a great many lives. Detailed studies of the major famines of the last two centuries have repeatedly found that the region concerned held enough food to feed everybody in it through the worst months, and in several cases went on exporting food while people were dying. What had collapsed was not supply but the ability of particular groups to command any part of it. A labourer whose wage is fixed and whose employer has no work for him cannot buy grain at any price, and if a rumour of shortage has doubled the price he is priced out long before the last sack has left the market. Famine on this account is a failure of entitlement rather than of harvest, and it falls on occupational groups rather than on regions: the landless labourer starves while the shopkeeper in the same street does not. The practical consequence is a large one. If the problem is absolute shortage, the response is to bring food in and wait. If the problem is purchasing power, the food is already in the region and the response is to put money or employment into the hands of the people who have lost theirs, which can usually be done faster and more cheaply. Governments that have understood this have stopped famines with public works and cash. Governments that have not have waited for ships.

For about a century, deaf children in most of Europe and North America were forbidden to sign. The policy had a name, oralism, and a date: an international congress of teachers of the deaf in 1880 resolved that speech was preferable to signs and that the two should never be combined. Almost none of the people who voted were themselves deaf. What followed was not a neglect of sign language but a sustained attempt to suppress it. Children were taught to lip-read and to produce sounds they could not hear, hands were tied or struck, and deaf teachers were removed from the schools that had employed them. The results were measured eventually, and they were poor: most pupils left with speech that strangers could not follow and a level of literacy well below that of their hearing contemporaries. The languages themselves survived, because the children taught them to one another in dormitories and playgrounds, out of sight of the staff. The reversal, when it came, was driven by linguists rather than by educators. Work from the 1960s onwards established what signers had always said and nobody in authority had troubled to test: that these were full languages, with grammar, with regional variation and with a history of their own, and not gestures accompanying a spoken language they imitated. Once that had been established the educational argument changed shape altogether, because a policy of replacing one language with another must be defended on quite different ground from a policy of replacing gestures with speech.

questions.stem: Although the open poll was defended at the time as the honest way of voting, and secrecy as something only a dishonest man could want, ----.

options.o1: it was the openness itself that made a voter's choice worth buying
options.o2: it was the secrecy of the ballot that made a voter's choice worth buying
options.o3: poll books went on being published in most constituencies for decades
options.o4: the clerk recorded each declaration in front of the whole room
options.o5: the argument took the better part of the nineteenth century to win

questions.why: Ödün bağlacı beklenenin tersini ister: açıklık dürüstlük değil, oyu satın alınabilir kılan şeydir.
questions.trap_note: Açıklıkla gizliliği değiştirir; parçanın bütün savı, satın almayı mümkün kılanın görünürlük olduğudur.

questions.stem: Because a man who buys a vote needs some proof that the vote was actually delivered to him, ----.

options.o1: making that proof impossible destroys the market without any policing at all
options.o2: making that proof impossible requires the state to police every polling station
options.o3: the open poll was abolished in most countries during the same decade
options.o4: employers were able to watch the voting from the back of the room
options.o5: a spoiled ballot is replaced by the clerk rather than corrected by him

questions.why: Alıcının kanıta muhtaç olması, kanıtı olanaksız kılmanın piyasayı kendiliğinden bitireceği anlamına gelir.
questions.trap_note: Aynı öncülden denetim gereğini çıkarır; oysa kanıtsızlık tam da denetime gerek bırakmayan çözümdür.

questions.stem: Not only did the mark on an industrial product tell a buyer whom to blame if the contents failed, ----.

options.o1: but it also gave the maker a reputation that could afterwards be lost
options.o2: but it also guaranteed that the contents were of a certain quality
options.o3: and the courts of the period treated it as a form of property
options.o4: so the presence of the seller was no longer of any importance
options.o5: although most goods were still bought from the person who made them

questions.why: Not only ... but also kalıbı ikinci bir işlev ister; markanın ikinci işlevi kaybedilebilir bir itibar kurmaktır.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın açıkça reddettiği şeyi söyler: marka içeriğin iyi olduğunu değil, kimin sorumlu olduğunu bildirir.

questions.stem: ----, the law would never have developed the doctrines of dilution and tarnishment that it now applies.

options.o1: Had a trademark remained nothing more than a warning to the buyer
options.o2: Had a trademark been treated as an asset from the very beginning
options.o3: If the courts of the nineteenth century had cared less about deception
options.o4: Because a mark with a reputation is worth a great deal of money
options.o5: Although no customer in an unrelated trade could possibly be confused

questions.why: Had + özne + V3 üçüncü tip koşuldur; bu doktrinler markanın mülk sayılmasından doğduğuna göre, uyarı olarak kalsaydı doğmazlardı.
questions.trap_note: Koşulu tersine çevirir: markanın baştan varlık sayılması bu doktrinleri engellemez, tam tersine üretir.

questions.stem: So much of the information in an archaeological site lies in the arrangement of its contents rather than in the objects themselves ----.

options.o1: that digging it up destroys most of what was there to be learned
options.o2: that digging it up recovers everything that was there to be learned
options.o3: and the objects afterwards sit in the cases of a museum
options.o4: because the soil above and below a find has been disturbed
options.o5: so excavators of the 1930s shovelled a great deal of it away

questions.why: So + nicelik yapısı that ile tamamlanır ve bir sonuç bildirir: bilgi düzendeyse, düzeni bozmak bilgiyi yok eder.
questions.trap_note: Yapıyı doğru tamamlar ama sonucu tersine çevirir; parçanın bütün sorunu kazının geri alınamaz oluşudur.

questions.stem: Leaving part of a famous site undug is a decision that would look like negligence in any other discipline, ----.

options.o1: whereas in archaeology it counts as a respectable piece of research policy
options.o2: whereas in archaeology it is regarded as the gravest kind of negligence
options.o3: since future methods will extract more from the same soil than present ones
options.o4: and several of the best-known sites have in fact been treated in this way
options.o5: because the record an excavator makes can never afterwards be checked

questions.why: whereas iki alanı karşı karşıya koyar; boşluk, başka yerde ihmal sayılacak kararın arkeolojideki karşılığını vermelidir.
questions.trap_note: Karşıtlık yerine aynılık kurar; whereas'ın istediği zıtlık ortadan kalkar.

questions.stem: Given that the regions in which the great famines occurred were holding enough food to feed everybody in them, ----.

options.o1: the explanation has to be sought in who was able to command any of it
options.o2: the explanation has to be sought in how much of it was being produced
options.o3: importing grain is the quickest way of bringing such a famine to an end
options.o4: the price of grain rose very steeply in the first weeks of the shortage
options.o5: shopkeepers and labourers were affected by the crisis to the same degree

questions.why: Yiyecek bölgede varsa açıklama miktarda olamaz; geriye ona kimin ulaşabildiği sorusu kalır.
questions.trap_note: Öncülü yok sayar: öncül tam da üretim miktarının yeterli olduğunu söylemektedir.

questions.stem: If a famine were really a matter of there being too little food in the region at all, ----.

options.o1: putting money into people's hands would do nothing whatever to stop it
options.o2: putting money into people's hands would be the quickest way of stopping it
options.o3: the labourers of the district would have been the last of all to suffer
options.o4: public works have been used to end famines in a number of countries
options.o5: the price of grain would have fallen as the shortage grew more severe

questions.why: İkinci tip koşul gerçeğe aykırı bir varsayım kurar: sorun gerçekten mutlak kıtlık olsaydı, para yaratmak bir şey çözmezdi.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın asıl savını yanlış koşula bağlar; para çözümü, sorun kıtlık değil alım gücü olduğu için işe yarar.

questions.stem: However thoroughly deaf children were drilled in speech during the century in which signing was forbidden, ----.

options.o1: most of them left school with speech that strangers could not follow
options.o2: most of them left school speaking as clearly as their hearing contemporaries
options.o3: the congress of 1880 had resolved that speech was preferable to signs
options.o4: deaf teachers were removed from the schools that had employed them
options.o5: the languages survived because the children taught them to one another

questions.why: However + zarf bir ödün kurar: çalışmanın yoğunluğu ne olursa olsun sonuç değişmemiştir.
questions.trap_note: Ödünü sonuçsuz bırakır; parça sonuçların kötü olduğunu ölçülmüş bir bulgu olarak verir.

questions.stem: Once linguists had shown that the signed languages were languages in the full sense and not gestures attached to speech, ----.

options.o1: the educational argument had to be conducted on quite different ground
options.o2: the educational argument went on being conducted in exactly the old terms
options.o3: the congress of 1880 was attended almost entirely by hearing teachers
options.o4: children had gone on signing to each other out of sight of the staff
options.o5: the policy of oralism had already been in force for about a century

questions.why: Parçanın son cümlesi bunu söyler: bir dili başka bir dille değiştirmek, el hareketlerini konuşmayla değiştirmekten başka bir zemin ister.
questions.trap_note: Bulgunun sonucunu siler; kanıt değiştiğinde tartışmanın zemini de değişmek zorundadır.

questions.stem: Secrecy here is not a right the voter may waive but a duty the state imposes on him for everybody else's protection.

options.o1: Burada gizlilik, seçmenin vazgeçebileceği bir hak değil, devletin herkesin korunması için ona yüklediği bir ödevdir.
options.o2: Burada gizlilik, devletin seçmene yüklediği bir ödev değil, onun dilerse vazgeçebileceği bir haktır.
options.o3: Seçmen gizlilik hakkından vazgeçtiğinde devlet onu herkesin korunması adına cezalandırır.
options.o4: Devlet, seçmenin gizlilik hakkını korumakla yükümlüdür ve bu yükümlülükten vazgeçemez.
options.o5: Gizlilik hem seçmenin bir hakkı hem de devletin ona yüklediği bir ödev sayılmaktadır.

questions.why: not X but Y kalıbı hakkı dışlar, ödevi koyar; çeviride bu sıra korunmalıdır.
questions.trap_note: Kalıbın iki ucunu değiştirir; aynı sözcüklerle cümlenin tersi söylenmiş olur.

questions.stem: The wrong being punished was deceiving the public, not taking something from the manufacturer.

options.o1: Cezalandırılan haksızlık, üreticiden bir şey almak değil, halkı yanıltmaktı.
options.o2: Cezalandırılan haksızlık, halkı yanıltmak değil, üreticiden bir şey almaktı.
options.o3: Halkı yanıltan üreticiler, kendilerinden bir şey alınarak cezalandırılıyordu.
options.o4: Üreticiden bir şey almak, halkı yanıltmaktan daha ağır bir haksızlık sayılıyordu.
options.o5: Halkın yanıltılması, üreticinin uğradığı zarar kanıtlanmadıkça cezalandırılmıyordu.

questions.why: Cümle neyin cezalandırıldığını açıkça ayırır: haksızlık halka karşıdır, üreticiye karşı değil.
questions.trap_note: İki haksızlığı yer değiştirir; markanın tüketici korumasından mülkiyete kayışı tam da bu ayrımda saklıdır.

questions.stem: No later scholar can go back and check a question that the excavator did not think to ask.

options.o1: Sonraki hiçbir araştırmacı geri dönüp kazıcının sormayı akıl etmediği bir soruyu denetleyemez.
options.o2: Sonraki araştırmacılar geri dönüp kazıcının sormayı akıl etmediği soruları denetleyebilir.
options.o3: Kazıcının sorduğu soruları sonraki araştırmacıların denetlemesi mümkün değildir.
options.o4: Kazıcı, sonraki araştırmacıların soracağı soruları önceden kestirmek zorundadır.
options.o5: Sonradan sorulan sorular, kazı sırasında sorulanlardan daha güvenilir sayılmaz.

questions.why: Cümle mutlak bir olanaksızlık bildirir: kayda geçmemiş bir soru sonradan denetlenemez.
questions.trap_note: Olumsuzluğu düşürür; aynı cümleyi bir olanak bildirisine çevirince parçanın savı yok olur.

questions.stem: Kıtlık, hasadın değil hak ediş düzeninin çökmesidir; bu yüzden bölgelere değil meslek gruplarına iner.

options.o1: A famine is the collapse not of the harvest but of the system of entitlement, which is why it falls on occupational groups rather than on regions.
options.o2: A famine is the collapse not of the system of entitlement but of the harvest, which is why it falls on regions rather than on occupational groups.
options.o3: A famine collapses both the harvest and the system of entitlement, and falls on regions and occupational groups alike.
options.o4: Where the harvest fails, the system of entitlement collapses with it and whole regions are affected.
options.o5: Occupational groups suffer in a famine only when the harvest of their own region has failed.

questions.why: Cümlede iki karşıtlık art arda gelir ve ikincisi birincinin sonucudur; çeviri ikisini de aynı yönde taşımalıdır.
questions.trap_note: Her iki karşıtlığı birden ters çevirir; yapı aynı kaldığı için değişiklik gözden kaçar.

questions.stem: 1880'de toplanan kongrede oy kullananların neredeyse hiçbiri sağır değildi.

options.o1: Almost none of those who voted at the congress held in 1880 were themselves deaf.
options.o2: Almost all of those who voted at the congress held in 1880 were themselves deaf.
options.o3: Hardly anybody who was deaf was allowed to attend the congress held in 1880.
options.o4: Those who were deaf voted against the resolution passed by the congress of 1880.
options.o5: The congress of 1880 was the first at which deaf teachers were able to vote.

questions.why: 'Neredeyse hiçbiri ... değildi' yapısı bir yokluk bildirir; İngilizcede bunu almost none karşılar.
questions.trap_note: Niceliği tersine çevirir; almost none ile almost all arasındaki fark cümlenin bütün yükünü taşır.

questions.stem: Bir dili başka bir dille değiştirme siyaseti, el hareketlerini konuşmayla değiştirme siyasetinden başka bir zeminde savunulmak zorundadır.

options.o1: A policy of replacing one language with another has to be defended on quite different ground from a policy of replacing gestures with speech.
options.o2: A policy of replacing gestures with speech has to be defended on quite different ground from a policy of replacing one language with another.
options.o3: Replacing one language with another and replacing gestures with speech are defended on precisely the same ground.
options.o4: A policy of replacing gestures with speech cannot be defended on any ground whatever.
options.o5: Those who defend the replacing of one language with another rarely mention gestures at all.

questions.why: Cümlede savunma yükü dilin yerine başka bir dil koyan siyasete aittir; karşılaştırmanın yönü korunmalıdır.
questions.trap_note: Karşılaştırmanın iki ucunu değiştirir; hangi siyasetin daha ağır bir gerekçe istediği tersine döner.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the open poll was originally presented as ----.

options.o1: a protection against fraud at the polling place
options.o2: a means of letting landlords know how tenants voted
options.o3: a temporary arrangement until secrecy could be organised
options.o4: a concession demanded by employers and creditors
options.o5: the cheapest way of conducting a large election

questions.why: Parça açık oylamanın sunuluş biçimini verir: sahteciliğe karşı bir güvence olarak savunulmuştur.
questions.trap_note: Açık oylamanın gerçek sonucunu, savunulma gerekçesi sanır; parça bunu 'tam tersi etki' diye ayırır.

questions.stem: It is clear from the passage that the argument for a secret ballot was hard to win because ----.

options.o1: it had to be made against a principle people genuinely held
options.o2: the corruption it was meant to end was difficult to prove
options.o3: most voters preferred to declare their choice in public
options.o4: the printing of uniform ballot papers was expensive
options.o5: landlords and employers controlled the legislature

questions.why: Parça güçlüğü adlandırır: savunulan şey basit bir yolsuzluk değil, gerçekten benimsenmiş bir dürüstlük ilkesiydi.
questions.trap_note: Güçlüğü kanıt sorununa bağlar; parça ise karşı tarafta ilkeli bir sav bulunduğunu söyler.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the rule replacing a spoiled ballot rather than correcting it ----.

options.o1: exists to stop a voter from producing evidence of his choice
options.o2: exists to spare the voter the embarrassment of a mistake
options.o3: was introduced before the secret ballot itself was adopted
options.o4: has little to do with the design of the modern ballot
options.o5: makes the counting of votes considerably quicker

questions.why: Parça sayılan kuralların ortak amacını verir: seçmenin nasıl oy verdiğini kanıtlayamaması.
questions.trap_note: Kuralı seçmenin duygularıyla açıklar; parça 'seçmenin duyguları etrafında kurulmamıştır' diyerek bunu dışlar.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.o1: The secret ballot was adopted to make vote-buying unprovable, and its rules bind the voter as well as everybody else.
options.o2: Voters in the nineteenth century were intimidated by employers, landlords and creditors alike.
options.o3: Privacy at the polling station is a right that every voter is entitled to give up.
options.o4: The open poll survived for so long because nobody had thought of an alternative.
options.o5: Elections became honest only once poll books ceased to be published.

questions.why: Parça iki şeyi birlikte kurar: kanıtı olanaksız kılma mantığı ve gizliliğin vazgeçilemez bir ödeve dönüşmesi.
questions.trap_note: Parçadaki örnekleri ana fikir yerine koyar; baskı, savın kendisi değil, dayanağıdır.

questions.stem: It is clear from the passage that what industrial production took away from the buyer was ----.

options.o1: somebody who could be found and held answerable
options.o2: the ability to judge the quality of goods by inspection
options.o3: any choice between competing makers of the same article
options.o4: the right to bring an action in the courts of the day
options.o5: the chance to buy goods made in his own district

questions.why: Parça alıcının korumasını satıcının varlığına bağlar; sanayi üretimi tam da bu varlığı ortadan kaldırmıştır.
questions.trap_note: Kaybı muayene becerisine bağlar; parçada korumanın kaynağı muayene değil, sorumlunun bulunabilmesidir.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the mark on a product told the buyer ----.

options.o1: who would answer for the contents, not how good they were
options.o2: how good the contents were, not who would answer for them
options.o3: where the factory that had made it was situated
options.o4: whether the article had been inspected before sale
options.o5: which of several competing articles was the cheaper

questions.why: Parça bunu doğrudan yazar: marka içeriğin iyi olduğunu söylemez, kimin sorumlu olduğunu söyler.
questions.trap_note: İki işlevi değiştirir; markanın kalite güvencesi sayılması parçanın düzelttiği yaygın yanılgıdır.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that doctrines such as dilution are difficult to justify by the original purpose of the law because ----.

options.o1: they operate where no buyer stands to be misled at all
options.o2: they protect manufacturers who have no reputation to lose
options.o3: they were invented by courts rather than by legislatures
options.o4: they apply only to goods sold a long way from the factory
options.o5: they make a mark harder to enforce than it once was

questions.why: Yasanın kökenindeki amaç halkın yanıltılmasını önlemektir; sulandırma ise kimsenin yanılmadığı yerde işler.
questions.trap_note: Güçlüğü itibarsız üreticilere bağlar; parçanın sorunu korunanın kim olduğu değil, ortada yanıltılan bir alıcının bulunmayışıdır.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.o1: A law made to protect buyers now protects a valuable asset, and the two purposes no longer point the same way.
options.o2: Trademark law should be repealed, since it no longer protects anybody from being deceived.
options.o3: Industrial production made it impossible for buyers to know who had made their goods.
options.o4: Nineteenth-century courts understood trademarks better than modern ones do.
options.o5: A mark with a reputation is the most valuable property a company can own.

questions.why: Parça yasanın kökenini ve bugünkü gerekçesini karşılaştırır ve ikisinin artık her zaman örtüşmediğini söyler.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın vermediği sonuca atlar: metin bazı yeni doktrinlerin gerekli olduğunu açıkça kabul eder.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the information an archaeological site carries lies chiefly in ----.

options.o1: the way its contents are positioned in relation to one another
options.o2: the objects that are eventually placed in museum cases
options.o3: the notebooks kept by the excavators of the 1930s
options.o4: the seeds, pollen and residues recovered from the soil
options.o5: the dates that modern methods are able to establish

questions.why: Parça ayrımı açıkça kurar: bilgi nesnelerde değil, nesnelerin düzeninde, yani katman ve ilişkilerdedir.
questions.trap_note: Nesneleri bilginin kendisi sanır; parça bunları bağlamından koparılmış kalıntılar olarak anar.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that leaving a site partly undug is defended on the ground that ----.

options.o1: later excavators will be able to read more from the same soil
options.o2: the sites in question are too large to be dug in one season
options.o3: museums have no room for the objects that would be found
options.o4: the public interest in such sites has declined in recent years
